passage:
Nitin, come and sit by your Dada Kishore. When I was ten, my friend Ramu told me he was scared of the dark and still slept with a lantern. "Swear you won't tell," he said. I swore. I felt so important, carrying that secret like a gold coin in my pocket. When boys called him a baby, I never said a word. It was heavy, but it was his.
Then one monsoon he whispered a different secret: he was going to swim across the swollen river to prove he wasn't a coward. My chest went tight. That night I told my father. He went straight to Ramu's house, and both fathers sat with Ramu till late. Ramu didn't speak to me for a week. But he was safe.

qa.q: What secret did Ramu first tell Kishore?
qa.a: Ramu told him he was scared of the dark and still slept with a lantern.

qa.q: How did young Kishore feel carrying Ramu's first secret?
qa.a: He felt proud and important, like carrying a gold coin, but also weighed down when the boys called Ramu a baby.

qa.q: What choice did young Kishore make about the river secret, and why was it right?
qa.a: He told his father that same night, because Ramu's plan could have got him hurt, and a secret about danger belongs with a grown-up.

qa.q: How did Ramu react after the fathers sat with him, and why?
qa.a: Ramu didn't speak to Kishore for a week, probably feeling betrayed, but he was safe.

grounding: A grandfather recalls feeling proud and burdened by a friend's secret as a boy, and knowing that a secret about danger had to go to an adult.

passage:
The school bus was stuck in rain-soaked traffic, windows fogged, forty children shouting songs. Rashmi leaned close so only Simran could hear. "We're moving to Chennai after the exams. Don't tell anyone. I want to tell them myself."
Simran nodded hard, feeling proud and heavy at the same time. For the rest of the ride she hugged her bag and said nothing when a boy asked why Rashmi looked sad.
She thought of what Mummy always said: secrets that make someone unsafe must go to a grown-up. This one wasn't unsafe. It was just sad, and it was Rashmi's to tell.
When the bus finally reached school, Simran squeezed Rashmi's hand. "Tell me when you're ready to tell them. I'll sit next to you."

qa.q: Where did Rashmi tell Simran the secret?
qa.a: On the school bus, stuck in rain-soaked traffic.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Rashmi shared the secret?
qa.a: She felt proud to be trusted and heavy with it at the same time.

qa.q: How did Simran decide whether to keep the secret?
qa.a: She remembered Mummy's rule that unsafe secrets go to a grown-up, saw that this one was sad but not unsafe, and kept it.

qa.q: What might Rashmi feel when Simran offers to sit next to her?
qa.a: Rashmi would likely feel supported and less alone about the move.

grounding: On a noisy, delayed bus a girl feels proud and burdened holding Rashmi's secret, and judges that it is sad rather than unsafe, so it is hers to keep.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.
At break, Dolma whispered a secret to Rekha. I don't know what it was, only that Rekha came back glowing, standing a little taller.
By the last period she looked worried. Two girls kept asking, "What did Dolma tell you?" Rekha pressed her lips together and shook her head.
After class she came to my desk. "Ma'am, do you have to keep a secret forever?"
I told her most secrets, like a surprise or a crush, are for keeping, and that's what good friends do. But a secret about someone being hurt or in danger must go to a grown-up, and that isn't betrayal.
She thought hard, then smiled. "Mine's a keeping one." She skipped off to find Dolma.

qa.q: What did Rekha ask the teacher after class?
qa.a: She asked, "Ma'am, do you have to keep a secret forever?"

qa.q: How did Rekha seem to feel about holding Dolma's secret?
qa.a: Rekha seemed proud to be trusted, standing taller, but also burdened and worried as the other girls kept asking.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Rekha?
qa.a: The teacher explained which secrets are for keeping and that secrets about someone being hurt or in danger must go to a grown-up.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel knowing Rekha refused to tell the other girls?
qa.a: Dolma would likely feel safe and grateful, knowing Rekha can be trusted.

grounding: A teacher notes a child feeling proud and burdened by a friend's secret, and learning that only safety secrets must go to an adult.

passage:
Wednesday
At the bus stop Ujjwal told me a HUGE secret. His ammi is going to have a baby! Nobody knows yet. He said, "Only you, Imran, because you're my best friend."
I felt like a king all day, carrying a golden box.
But it's heavy too. At lunch Faiz asked why Ujjwal was so happy, and I nearly said it. I stuffed a whole samosa in my mouth instead.
At home Ammi asked why I was quiet. I said I was keeping a secret for Ujjwal. She said, "Good. A happy secret is his to share. But if a friend tells you someone is hurting them, you tell me. That kind isn't for keeping."
This one's happy. I'm keeping it.

qa.q: What secret did Ujjwal tell Imran?
qa.a: His ammi is going to have a baby.

qa.q: How did Imran feel carrying Ujjwal's secret?
qa.a: Imran felt proud and special, like carrying a golden box, but also burdened because it was hard not to say it.

qa.q: What did Imran's Ammi teach him about secrets?
qa.a: She said a happy secret is Ujjwal's to share, but a secret about someone being hurt must be told to her.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel if Imran keeps the secret till the baby is born?
qa.a: Ujjwal would feel he can truly trust Imran, and their friendship would grow stronger.

grounding: A child's diary shows pride and burden in keeping a friend's happy secret, and learning that safety secrets go to an adult.

passage:
Behind the grain store in the village, Ankita lifted a loose brick and showed Preeti a small tin full of coins.
"I'm saving for a sari for my Amma, for Diwali," Ankita whispered. "It's a surprise. Don't tell anyone. Promise?"
"Promise," Preeti said, and felt as if she'd been handed something precious.
All week she guarded it. When Ankita's Amma asked Preeti why the girls kept going behind the store, Preeti's cheeks burned. "Just playing, Kaki."
That night, she asked her Dadi, "Is it wrong to keep a secret from a grown-up?"
Dadi stroked her hair. "A surprise is a kind secret. Keep it. But if a friend's secret is about someone hurting her, or her being in danger, you come straight to me."
Preeti nodded, relieved. The sari secret was a kind one.

qa.q: What was Ankita saving for?
qa.a: She was saving for a sari for her Amma, for Diwali.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's cheeks burn when Ankita's Amma asked about the grain store?
qa.a: Preeti felt nervous and torn, proud to protect the surprise but uncomfortable keeping it from a grown-up.

qa.q: What did Dadi explain that helped Preeti?
qa.a: Dadi explained that a surprise is a kind secret to keep, but a secret about someone being hurt or in danger must come straight to her.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel on Diwali if the surprise works?
qa.a: Ankita would feel proud and happy, and she would trust Preeti even more for keeping the secret.

grounding: It shows a child treasuring a friend's surprise secret and learning from her grandmother that safety secrets must go to an adult.

passage:
At break time in the school playground in Leeds, Amara pulled Fatima behind the climbing frame. "Promise you won't tell anyone? I still sleep with my old teddy. Every night."
Fatima nodded hard. "I promise."
All afternoon she felt tall and important. Amara had told her, not anyone else. But it was heavy too. When Chloe said at lunch that teddies were for babies, Fatima had to bite her lip very hard to keep quiet.
At home she asked Mum, "How do you know if you should keep a secret?"
Mum stopped chopping onions. "If it's a happy or private secret, you keep it. If it's a secret that means someone could get hurt, you tell a grown-up, even if you promised."
Fatima thought about the teddy. Nobody could get hurt by a teddy.
She kept it. She felt proud every time she saw Amara.

qa.q: What secret did Amara tell Fatima?
qa.a: Amara still sleeps with her old teddy every night.

qa.q: How did Fatima feel about being told the secret?
qa.a: Fatima felt proud and important to be trusted, but also burdened, biting her lip to keep quiet when Chloe teased about teddies.

qa.q: What rule did Mum give Fatima about secrets?
qa.a: Keep happy or private secrets, but tell a grown-up about any secret that means someone could get hurt, even after promising.

qa.q: What might it mean to Amara that Fatima kept quiet?
qa.a: Amara can feel safe and trust Fatima more, knowing a private thing was held carefully.

grounding: Shows a child proud and burdened by a friend's secret, learning to hold it while knowing that secrets about harm must go to an adult.
